The outcomes of the trials were defined inconsistently, ranging from confirmed HIV diagnosis to self-reported reactive HIV self-testing (HIVST) results, self-reported positivity, or unclear definitions. Despite this, the results were generally similar across individual trials, although the strength of the effect varied. In two trials, the direction of the effect favored the standard of care. 2. All trials focused on HIV self-testing. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that downgrading for indirectness was unnecessary because the intervention and populations were sufficiently similar to those in hepatitis C virus self-testing (HCVST). 3. The original sample size in the meta-analysis did not represent the effective cluster-adjusted sample size. 4. In the meta-analysis, studies such as Chanda (2017), Ortblad (2019), and Wray (2018) included more than one intervention arm involving HIVST. These arms were combined for analysis. Cluster-adjusted analyses were included for cluster-randomized trials. 5. Six individual randomized trials were included. Downgrading occurred once due to a 4% overall loss to follow-up (LTFU), with 26% in the intervention arm and 50% in the control arm. Self-testing was found to be acceptable and effective in various settings, including among drug users, young offenders, and the general population. However, challenges such as confusion with instructional steps, finger-pricking, and sample collection were noted.
